Welcome to SquatClient, a graphical MU client with a TinyFugue-style scripting language and Lua. This help browser is built into the app: it works offline and everything in it is searchable.
Want to connect to a game? See Connecting and worlds.
Want your sessions to survive closing the app? See Squatter.
Looking for a key? See Keyboard shortcuts.
Want to write triggers and macros? Start with the scripting language, then Lua scripting.
Open help type /help, press F1 (Cmd-? on macOS), choose Help in the menu, or click the ? button
Open a topic /help def, /help keys, /help squatter (a leading / is fine: /help /def)
Search type in the search box, or /help some words
Move around click the topic tree, follow links, or press Alt-Left and Alt-Right for back and forward
Jump to the search box press /
Try an example every code block has Copy and Insert into input buttons; Insert puts the text on your input line without sending it

By default a world connects Direct and ends when you quit. To keep connections running while the app is closed, set up a squatter and choose it in a world's Connect via setting; see Squatters and routing.

A squatter is a saved remote relay: a squatterd you run on a server. You can save many squatters, for example home-vps and work-box.
Each world chooses how it connects with its Connect via setting:
Direct: straight from this computer to the game. The connection ends when the app closes.
A saved squatter: the squatter holds the game connection. It survives closing the app, and when you reattach everything you missed is replayed.
Different worlds can therefore use different squatters, and some can be direct, all at the same time.
There is one hop for now: client, squatter, game. Chaining squatters, or a squatter going out through a proxy, is planned for later and is not available yet.
Star Trek home-vps held by home-vps; still connected tomorrow
Work MUSH work-box held by work-box
Quick test Direct ends when you quit
On the server run ./squatterd pair and note the one-time code and the fingerprint.
In SquatClient open the squatters dialog, choose Add a squatter, and enter the name, host, port and code.
Confirm that the TLS fingerprint shown matches the one squatterd pair printed, then Trust and pair.
In each world that should use it, set Connect via to the new squatter.

then add the squatter as 127.0.0.1 port 10327. On the server start squatterd with --bind 127.0.0.1 --insecure-loopback as described in the squatterd README.
/suspend and /detach detach the squatter-held sessions; they keep running. An ended session is just history: nothing reconnects automatically, and the squatter stores no game passwords. See Squatter.

A world is a saved connection. Open the world manager with Ctrl-O, the menu (Session, Worlds) or the tab-bar button. Worlds are stored in a file in the SquatClient configuration folder; passwords never are.

Tick Use TLS when the game offers a TLS port. Certificates are verified strictly by default. Some games use a self-signed certificate; for those, tick Skip certificate verification, understanding that it removes protection against someone impersonating the game.

UTF-8 is the default and handles accented letters, emoji and box-drawing characters. Some older games send Latin-1; if you see garbled accents, switch that world to Latin-1. You can set the default for new connections in Settings.
If a world has a login template the client sends it for you after connecting. A typical MUSH template is:

Game passwords are saved in the operating system keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service on Linux), never in the worlds file; the file only records that a password exists. If the keychain cannot be reached, connecting to a world that needs a password fails with an error rather than sending an empty password. A squatter never stores your game passwords either: your client sends the login.

Each connection is a tab. Press Alt-1 to Alt-9 to switch, or Ctrl-Tab and Ctrl-Shift-Tab to cycle. A badge on a tab shows unread lines in background connections, and the status bar shows how many are active. Closing a tab disconnects it; an ended tab stays until you dismiss it, with the reason and the last text received.
The scripting language can also define and connect worlds; see /addworld, /connect, /world and /fg in Commands.

squatterd is a small optional program that holds your game connections for you, in the spirit of screen or TinyFugue on a shell account. You run it on a machine that stays on. When you close SquatClient the game connection stays up, squatterd keeps recording what the game says, and the next time you attach it replays everything you missed and carries on live.
You do not need a squatter to use SquatClient. Without one, connections are direct and end when you quit the app.
It never logs in for you and stores no game passwords. Your client sends the login lines.
It never reconnects automatically. If the game connection ends, the session is shown as ended with the reason, and it stays ended until you dismiss it.
On the machine that will hold your sessions (the engine repository builds the binary with make build):

The default port is 10327, the connection is TLS, and data lives in ~/.squatterd. To see the other options use ./squatterd --help; for example --bind limits the address it listens on and --data-dir moves its files.
Pairing lets this copy of SquatClient talk to your squatter. It happens once per device.
It prints a one-time pairing code such as ABCD-EFGH (valid for ten minutes), the TLS fingerprint, and a host and port hint.
In SquatClient open the squatters dialog (the tab-bar button), choose Add a squatter, and enter a name, the host, the port (10327 unless you changed it) and the pairing code. Press Pair.
Compare the fingerprint SquatClient shows with the one squatterd pair printed. If they match, press Trust and pair. If they differ, press Reject: something is between you and your server.

The squatter makes its own TLS certificate, so there is no certificate authority to vouch for it. SquatClient therefore uses trust on first use: you confirm the fingerprint once, and from then on that exact fingerprint is pinned. If it ever changes, the connection is refused. Only pair devices you trust: anyone who can pair can open connections to any host from the squatter machine, and ./squatterd revoke <deviceId> removes a device.

In the world manager set Connect via to your squatter. Sessions you open that way live on the squatter. You can save several squatters and route different worlds through different ones; see Squatters and routing.

Type /suspend (or /detach) to let go of squatter-held sessions while leaving them running: the client goes idle, the sessions keep recording, and you resume later by attaching again, when everything you missed is replayed. Direct sessions cannot outlive the app, so for them /suspend can only hide the window and the connections stay live. If both kinds are open only the squatter-held sessions are detached.
Note: this behaviour is specified in the project design; if your build prints /suspend (not available), simply close the app, and the squatter-held sessions carry on regardless.

When a game closes the connection, resets it or cannot be reached, the session becomes ended. The tab shows the reason, the time and the last text received, and the full history is kept. Choose Connect again to open a fresh connection or Dismiss to remove it. Nothing reconnects by itself.
Transport: TLS with a pinned self-signed certificate.
Authentication: your client holds an ed25519 key; the squatter remembers its public key.
Pairing codes are single use and expire; repeated wrong codes lock out the sender for five minutes.
If you reach the squatter through an ssh tunnel, point the client at the loopback address as described in the squatterd README.

Tab bar: one tab per connection, plus buttons for worlds, quick connect, squatters, search, settings and help.
Output pane: what the game says, plus your own typed lines and system messages.
Input line: where you type. Lines starting with / are commands, anything else is sent to the game.
Status bar: connection state, activity in other tabs, the pause marker, any fields your scripts add, and the clock.

Text keeps the colours and styles the game sends: bold, dim, italic, underline, strikethrough, blink and reverse. Colours can be the 16 theme colours, the 256-colour xterm palette, or 24-bit truecolour, and all of UTF-8 is displayed. Links the game marks up, and bare http:// and https:// addresses (if enabled in Settings), are clickable and open in your system browser. Only web addresses are ever opened.
Select text with the mouse and copy it as usual.
Recent output is kept in memory, up to the scrollback lines setting; older history is fetched on demand when you scroll up. Use PageUp and PageDown to scroll, or the mouse wheel.

When you scroll up, live output pauses so the text you are reading does not move (if Pause output when scrolled up is on). The status bar shows --More-- with a count of lines that arrived meanwhile. Press End (when the output has focus) or the jump button to return to live output. This replaces TinyFugue's --More-- prompt.

Press Cmd-F or Ctrl-Shift-F (Ctrl-F when the output has focus) to open the search bar. It offers previous and next match, case sensitivity and regular expressions, and searches the whole scrollback of the current tab.
The input line understands the Emacs editing keys TinyFugue users know. The full list is in Keyboard shortcuts. Highlights:
Home/End or Ctrl-A/Ctrl-E move to the start or end.
Ctrl-W and Alt-D delete words; Ctrl-K and Ctrl-U delete to the end or the whole line; Ctrl-Y pastes the last deletion.
Shift-Enter inserts a new line so you can write several lines before sending.
Pasting several lines sends them one by one.

Up and Down (or Ctrl-P and Ctrl-N) walk through lines you sent earlier. If you typed something first, only lines starting with it are offered, so typing /def and pressing Up finds your last /def command.
When the game turns off echo (for a password prompt) the input becomes a masked password field with a lock icon, history is disabled and what you type is not recorded.

Each connection has a tab. Use Alt-1 to Alt-9 or Ctrl-Tab to switch. Unread lines in background tabs show as a badge, and with desktop notifications on you also get notified. The small x on a tab disconnects it, or dismisses it if it has already ended.

Pick a theme in Settings: Dark, Light or High contrast. A theme sets the text and background colours, the 16 ANSI colours and the colours of the window chrome. You can import your own theme as JSON. If some colour combinations are hard to read, set Minimum contrast (4.5 is the WCAG AA level) and the client nudges colours to meet it. The client respects your system's reduce motion preference.

By default SquatClient shows UTF-8 text with xterm-256 and 24-bit truecolour. Bold text uses bright colours makes bold text switch to the bright variant of the 8 basic colours, as in many terminals. In scripts you can use all of these colours; see Attributes.

Dialogs trap keyboard focus and close with Escape, controls have labels, and Screen-reader mode announces new lines to assistive technology. A "Skip to input" link is the first thing a keyboard user reaches.

> SquatClient's scripting language is an original implementation, inspired by and designed to be closely compatible with TinyFugue ("tf"). TinyFugue was written by Ken Keys (<https://tinyfugue.sourceforge.net>). Thank you, Ken, and thank you to the TinyFugue community for decades of documentation, scripts and answers. See About and credits.

SquatClient contains no TinyFugue source code and bundles none of its help text; it follows TinyFugue's documented behaviour and improves on it in a few places. If you know TinyFugue you will feel at home; the differences are listed in Compatibility notes.
Lines that start with / are commands; everything else is text for the game. A script is a plain .tf file of commands that you /load.
/set greeting=Hello /echo %greeting, world /def -t'* tells you: *' -ahCgreen tell = /echo Got a tell from %P1
A macro is a named command list made with /def. With -t it becomes a trigger that fires on matching game text; with -h it is a hook that fires on an event.
Variables are set with /set and read with %name or %{name}.
The rest of this section is the reference for the language, one page per chapter. Use /help name to jump straight to a command or function, for example /help def, /help strlen or /help expressions.
Use the Insert into input button on any example to try it.
Commands, the list of everything starting with /.
lua squat plugins gopher-lua scripting api

SquatClient embeds Lua 5.1 as a sandboxed second scripting language alongside the TinyFugue-style language. Use Lua for larger, structured plugins and TF for quick triggers and for scripts you already have; the two can call each other.

Everything lives in the global table squat. Plugins are .lua files in the plugins folder of the SquatClient scripts directory and are loaded at start. Type /reload to reload them. You can also try code directly:
The following pages are the full reference of the squat. API.
compatibility tinyfugue differences tf matrix out of scope gui not implemented
A short version of what matches TinyFugue, what is intentionally different, and what is out of scope. The full, authoritative matrix follows in the pages below this one.
The command syntax and most commands: /def, /set, /let, /if, /while, /for, /eval, /test, /repeat, /quote, /load, /require and more.
Macro options -t -m -h -p -n -F -g -a -P -b -w -E -c, and glob, simple and regexp patterns.
The expression language, its operators and most functions, and the hook names.
The Emacs-style editing keys and history.
Inside expressions, %x and %1 are variable references, never re-parsed as text. That prevents text from the game from injecting commands.
=~ and !~ compare strings exactly; =/ and !/ are glob matches. There is no % operator: use mod().
Triggers fire deterministically: by priority, then definition order, and only one macro per priority unless -F is given. TinyFugue picks randomly among equals.
Every glob wildcard of a trigger is available as %P1, %P2...
A script file that contains a line that is not a command is an error; scripts never send text by accident.
Backquote command substitution is not provided, because it implied a shell.
Colour attributes also accept 256-colour indices, the rgb cube, grayN and #rrggbb truecolour.
Every script run has a step budget, a time limit and nesting limits so a runaway macro cannot freeze the client.

SquatClient is a graphical client. Features that exist in TinyFugue only because it ran in a terminal are not implemented and not planned: line wrapping variables (wrap, wrapsize...), the terminal --More-- prompt (replaced by pause-when-scrolled-up), screen modes (/visual, /redraw), terminal signals, terminal geometry, and the keyboard-buffer functions. Scripts that use them still load: the commands and variables are accepted and ignored. Shell commands (/sh) are not available.

The compatibility matrix was written from the public TinyFugue manual and has not yet been verified against a reference tf binary, so read "Done" as "implemented to the documented intent". Some features are planned: /edit, /recordline, /watchdog, the stream functions (tfopen and friends) and %{-N} ranges.

SquatClient is a graphical MU client for desktop, with a TinyFugue-style scripting language, Lua, and optional persistent sessions through squatterd.

SquatClient's scripting language, and much of the overall design of the client, were inspired by TinyFugue ("tf"), written by Ken Keys (<https://tinyfugue.sourceforge.net>). TinyFugue defined how a good MU client works: worlds, macros, triggers, hooks, a status line and an Emacs-style input line. SquatClient's language is an original implementation designed to be closely compatible with it, and contains no TinyFugue code. Thank you to Ken Keys and to the TinyFugue community.

pkg/tf implements a TinyFugue-style MU client language. It is an original implementation inspired by TinyFugue's documented behaviour; it is not bug-for-bug compatible. Differences are listed in TF-COMPAT.md.
Scripts are plain text files (.tf). Everything below can be typed on the input line, put in a script and /loaded, or run by triggers and hooks.
A line that starts with / is a command. Any other line is text and is sent to the world (not expanded, unless /set sub=on).

A command line is split into statements at ; and at %;. Separators inside $[...], $(...) and %{...} do not split. /def, /repeat and /eval keep %; unsplit so that it separates statements when their body runs later:
/def greet = /echo hello %; /echo again ; the whole body is stored
A plain ; ends the /def itself. Text lines are never split at ;.

Script files: blank lines and lines starting with ; are ignored; a line ending in \ continues on the next line (leading blanks of the next line are dropped). Every other line must be a command (non-command lines in a file are an error: a script never sends text by accident). Blocks (/if, /while, /do, /for) may span lines and are collected until their /endif / /done.
Errors print as % message through the host and the script keeps going, except that an error inside a loop body ends the loop. At most 20 errors are shown per run.
Performed on the arguments of ordinary commands and on every statement of a macro body when it runs.
%name, %{name} variable (local first, then global); unset is empty
% all arguments as typed; %# their count; %0 the macro name
%PL %PR text left / right of the last regexp match; %L is the last positional parameter, %R a random one
%-N %{-N} %-L all parameters but the first N / but the last
%{sel-default} the default when the selector expands to nothing
%P0..%P9, %{P12} match parts: P0 the whole match, P1.. captures
%{?name} 1 if the variable is set, else 0
$(command) what the command echoed (lines joined by spaces); if it echoed nothing, its /return value
Substitution is a single pass: substituted text is not rescanned, so text from the MUD can never inject commands through %. /eval expands its arguments and then runs the result, which expands again:
/set cmd=/echo hi /eval %cmd ; runs /echo hi /eval /echo %%{x} ; first pass leaves %{x}, second pass expands it
Triggers receive % = the line, %1.. = its words, %P0 = the whole match, %P1.. = glob wildcards or regexp groups in order, %PL/%PR for regexp triggers.
Values are integers (int64), floats, or strings. Text that looks like a number is a number; arithmetic treats non-numeric text as 0. Truth: a non-zero number, or a non-empty non-numeric string.
== != equal: numeric when both sides are numbers, else string compare
=~ !~ exact string equal / not equal (never numeric)
< > <= >= numeric when both numbers, else string order
/ multiply, divide (integer division when both are integers; division by zero is an error)

Barewords are variables (x); name(args) calls a function; {x}, {1}, {}, {#} and %x, %1, %, %#, %{name} read variables and parameters without re-parsing the value as expression text (prefer these for script input). There is no % operator (use mod()); % is not interpolated inside string literals (use strcat). String literals use " or ' with \n \t \r \e \\ \" escapes. Numbers: 12, 1.5, .5, 1e3, 0x1f.
A user macro can be called like a function: /def add = /return {1} + {2} then $[add(2, 3)].
/set name=value (or /set name value) sets a global; if a local of that name exists in the running macro, the local is changed instead.
/let name=value creates/sets a local that lives until the macro returns.
/setenv name=value is /set plus marking it exported; /export name marks an existing one. /unset name. /listvar [glob]. /set alone lists everything.
Names are [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]. Values are strings that act as numbers when numeric.

Behavioural variables read by the interpreter: gag and hilite (set to 0 to disable gag/hilite effects), matching (default /def match mode), hiliteattr (attribute used by /hilite, default h), sub (on expands % in typed text), quiet, TZ (UTC or a fixed offset such as UTC+2, -0530, used by ftime/mktime), histsize. Others from TinyFugue are accepted as ordinary variables (see TF-COMPAT.md).
The host can export and import all globals as JSON (ExportVars, ImportVars).

The body is stored unexpanded and expanded each time the macro runs. Calling /name args runs it with %1.. set from args. A macro may also be a trigger, a hook, or a key binding. Options (no space between the letter and its value; quote values containing spaces with '..', ".." or {..}):
-t<pattern> trigger on received text matching the pattern
-m<glob\ simple\ regexp> pattern style (default glob, or $matching)
-h<HOOK [argpattern]> run when the hook fires (optional glob over the hook's arguments)
-n<shots> / -1 delete the macro after that many firings
-F fall-through: after firing, let lower-priority matches fire too
-a<attrs> highlight the whole line (see section 6); g in the attrs gags
-P<n><attrs> highlight part n (0 whole match, 1..9 capture/wildcard)
-b<key> / -k<key> bind to a key name (the engine delivers key names)
-E<expr> extra condition; must be true for the macro to fire
-c<percent> fire with that probability (0 or 100 = always)
glob matches the whole line: any text, ? one character, [a-z] / [^a-z] classes, {red|blue} alternatives, \ a literal. Write dragon to match anywhere. Each wildcard becomes %P1...
simple: the line must equal the pattern exactly.
regexp: Go (RE2) syntax, matches anywhere in the line, %P0.., %PL, %PR.

Dispatch: matching macros are ordered by priority (high first), then definition order. The first one fires; if it has -F the next fires too, and so on. Only one macro per priority level fires unless -F is used (a deliberate simplification: TF picks randomly among equals). A hook fires its macros the same way; hook arguments become %1...
/undefn N... remove by number shown in /list
/enable name... /disable name... extension: switch a macro off/on without deleting it
/trigger [-w world] text run triggers as if text had arrived
/trigpc chance priority text like /trigger with a probability, only macros of at least that priority
/bind key = command, /unbind key, /dokey name key bindings; /dokey asks the host to perform a key action
Redefining a name replaces the macro and fires the REDEF hook. A macro name shadows a built-in command of the same name; /builtin name args runs the built-in.
An attribute string is a comma-separated list; each item is flag letters optionally followed by one colour clause:
d i u s f r dim, italic, underline, strike, flash/blink, reverse

Colours: black red green yellow blue magenta cyan white (0-7), bright + name (8-15), a palette index 0..255 (xterm-256), rgbRGB (6x6x6 cube, digits 0-5, e.g. rgb530), gray0..gray23, and 24-bit #rrggbb or #rgb.
/echo -aCred,u red underlined /echo -aC196 palette 196 /echo -aC#ff8800,BC#001122 truecolour on truecolour /def -t'*dragon*' -ahC#ff4040 dragon /def -mregexp -t'(\d+) gold' -P1BCyellow,C0 gold
Inline markup (/echo -p, echo(), encodeattr): @{attrs} changes the current attributes (they accumulate; @{n} resets), @@ is a literal @: /echo -p @{Cred}red@{n} plain @{C#00ff00}green.

/if (expr) commands /elseif (expr) commands /else commands /endif /while (expr) ; /do directly after the header is optional ... /done /do ... /while (expr) /for var first last commands /done /break /return [expr]
Commands after a header on the same line are the first statements of that body; separate statements with %; inside macro bodies:

(/let and /set store text: /let i=i+1 would store the string i+1; use $[...] to compute.) A typed line closes unfinished blocks at its end; in a script file an unfinished block is an error. Every run is limited (section 10).
/help lists them and /help name prints usage.
Output: /echo [-w world] [-a attrs] [-p] text, /send [-w world] text, /beep, /notify title | body (extension), /gag, /hilite.

Timers: /repeat [-w world] -<seconds|m:s|h:m:s> <count> <command> runs a command repeatedly through the host's timer service (/repeat 3 cmd without a time runs it three times now); /ps lists timers, /kill id stops one.

/quote [-dsend|echo|exec] [prefix] 'file runs each line of a file (needs file access) and /quote [prefix] #command each line a command echoes; every line becomes prefix + line. Shell forms (!cmd, cmd ) are not available.
Worlds (need world access): /addworld [-Ttype] [-x] name [char pass] host port, /connect [world], /dc [world], /fg [world], /world name, /unworld, /listworlds [glob], /listsockets, /saveworld.
UI delegates (the host decides what they do): /limit /unlimit /relimit /recall /log /input /localecho /statusadd /statusedit /statusrm /dokey /histsize.

/restrict raises (never lowers) the restriction level: shell (always in force; there is no shell access), file (no /load /save /quote 'file /log), world (also no world/connection commands). The application sets the initial level (Options.Restrict).

Strings: strlen strcat strcmp strncmp strchr strrchr strstr strrep substr pad tolower toupper replace substitute ascii char (indices are in characters, 0 based; strchr(s, set) is the first position of any character of set, or -1; pad(s, w) right-justifies in w columns, a negative width left-justifies; replace(old, new, s) replaces every occurrence of old in s (TF argument order); substitute(text [, attrs [, inline]]) replaces the line being processed by a trigger).
Regexp: regmatch(pattern, string) returns 1/0 and sets %P0..%P9, %PL, %PR for the rest of the macro.
Math: abs sin cos tan asin acos atan exp ln log10 pow sqrt rand trunc mod (rand(n) is 0..n-1; rand(a, b) is inclusive).

Time: time() (Unix seconds), mktime(y,m,d,h,mi,s), ftime(format [, secs]) (strftime codes %Y %y %m %d %e %H %I %M %S %p %a %A %b %B %j %Z %z %s %F %T %R %D %c %n %t %%), idle([world]) seconds since last input, sidle([world]) since last send.

Misc: eval(str) (expand and run as commands, returns the echoed text), test(expr), whatis(v) (int, float, str), getopts(optstring [, args]) (sets locals optx, returns the remaining arguments), echo(str [, attrs [, inline [, world]]]), send(str [, world]), prompt(str), worldinfo([world,] field) (name host port character type tls connected), isconnected([world]), isopen, fgworld(), nactive(), columns(), lines(), winlines(), isatty(), systype().
Attributes: encodeattr(text, attrs), decodeattr(text) (markup to an ANSI string with 16/256/24-bit codes), stripattr(text) (remove markup and ANSI).

/def -hNAME [argpattern] name = body. Names: ACTIVITY ATCP BAMF BGTEXT BGTRIG CONFAIL CONFLICT CONNECT DISCONNECT GMCP ICONFAIL KILL LOAD LOADFAIL LOG LOGIN MAIL MORE NOMACRO OPTION102 PENDING PREACTIVITY PROCESS PROMPT PROXY REDEF RESIZE SEND SHADOW SHELL SIGHUP SIGTERM SIGUSR1 SIGUSR2 WORLD. The application fires them with FireHook(name, args...); the engine fires CONNECT DISCONNECT CONFAIL LOGIN WORLD SEND PROMPT ACTIVITY BGTEXT BGTRIG LOAD REDEF RESIZE GMCP. The interpreter itself fires SEND (before text is sent; a SEND hook that sends does not recurse), LOAD, LOADFAIL and REDEF. /hook NAME args fires a hook by hand; /hook lists names. Hook arguments are %1.., e.g. GMCP gets %1 = package, %2 = JSON.
Every top-level run (an input line, a received line, a hook, a key, a timer, one logical line of a loaded file) has:
a step budget (statements, loop iterations, expression evaluations, function calls; default 50 000),
a wall deadline on the host clock (default 2 s),
a macro nesting limit (default 64) and file nesting limit (16),
a 256 KB cap on any one string value.

Exceeding a limit aborts that run with % script budget exceeded: ...; the interpreter stays usable. When a received line is replayed from scrollback (live=false) no macro body runs, nothing is sent or notified, no shot is consumed and no variable is changed; only gag and highlight are computed.

; keep-alive every five minutes /def -hCONNECT on_connect = /repeat -300 100000 /send IDLE ; highlight tells and notify /def -mregexp -t'^(\w+) tells you: (.*)$' -P1Cbrightgreen,h tell = \ /notify Tell from %P1 | %P2 ; gag spam, but only from one world /def -wmain -t'\[Spam\]*' -g spam ; auto-loot with a condition and a 50% chance /def -t'* is dead.' -E'looting' -c50 loot = get all from corpse ; 256 and truecolour /def -t'*ALERT*' -a'BC#400000,C#ffe0e0,h' alert ; a helper with a return value /def max = /return {1} > {2} ? {1} : {2} /echo biggest: $[max(3, 9)]

See pkg/tf/doc.go and host.go: implement tf.Host (embed tf.NopHost), tf.New(host, tf.Options{...}), then Exec, OnLine(world, line, live), FireHook, Key, LoadFile/LoadString, Vars/GetVar/SetVar/ExportVars/ ImportVars, Macros. All calls are serialised; host callbacks must not call back into the interpreter.

Status legend: Done (works as described in TF-LANGUAGE.md), Partial (works with the stated difference), Planned (P2), GUI (replaced by a GUI feature, the host decides), N/A (not applicable to this client).

pkg/tf is a clean-room implementation inspired by TinyFugue's documented behaviour; it contains no TinyFugue code or help text. The checklist is the list in squatClient/docs/DESIGN.md section 3.2. Those lists were written from TinyFugue's cmdlist.h, funclist.h, hooklist.h, varlist.h; the semantics below were implemented from knowledge of the public manual, not verified against a reference binary yet (the oracle differential tests of DESIGN 3.5 are not set up), so treat every "Done" as "implemented to the documented intent". Where TF's exact behaviour was uncertain the most sensible semantics were chosen and are noted here.

Expression substitution % text substitution happens inside expressions Inside $[..], /if (..) etc. %x, %1, %, %{x} are variable references (never re-parsed as expression text); % is not interpolated in string literals. Removes a code-injection hazard from MUD text.
=~ !~ =/ !/ as defined by TF =~/!~: exact string equal / not equal. =//!/: glob match (pattern on the right). Regexps via regmatch() or -mregexp.
No modulo operator n/a use mod().
Trigger firing one random macro among equal priorities deterministic: priority desc, then definition order; the first fires, -F continues. Only one macro per priority level fires unless -F.
Glob captures none every wildcard of a glob trigger is %P1.. (%P0 the whole line).
Statement splitting text lines (not starting /) are never split at ;; /def, /repeat, /eval keep %; for later.
Script files non-command lines are sent as text non-command lines in a loaded file are an error (no accidental sends). Unclosed blocks in a file are an error.
Error handling errors are reported as % msg and execution continues, but an error inside a loop body ends the loop; max 20 errors shown per run.
/def of a built-in name the macro shadows the built-in; /builtin cmd reaches the built-in.
%{N} / %{-N} ranges %{-N} and %{N-} style ranges are not implemented. %0 is the macro name.
$(command) command substitution returns the echoed lines joined by spaces, else the /return value. Backquote cmd substitution is not implemented (it implied a shell).
Time zones system TZ TZ supports UTC and fixed offsets only (the package does no I/O, so no zoneinfo).
pad() positive width right-justifies, negative left-justifies, no truncation.
regmatch() POSIX-ish regexps Go RE2 syntax; returns 1/0 (not an offset).
eval() function runs the string as commands and returns the echoed text.
/hook enables/disables hooks lists hook names, or fires a hook by hand.
Budgets none every run has a step budget, wall deadline, nesting and string-size limits (section 11 of TF-LANGUAGE).

Colours 16/8 colours attribute strings also accept xterm-256 indices (C196), the rgbRGB cube, gray0..23 and truecolour #rrggbb. Attribute letters i (italic) and s (strike) are additions. B is bold and BC<colour> is a background (a bare B immediately followed by C always means background).
Extensions /notify, /enable, /disable, /builtin, /return, calling macros as functions, -E/-c on hooks.
Policy: terminal-only TinyFugue features are out of scope

SquatClient is a GUI client. Anything TinyFugue has only because it ran in a text terminal is not implemented and not planned. Scripts that use them still load: the commands/variables are accepted and ignored (no error), so a .tf file written for the terminal does not break here. Where a GUI equivalent exists, it is a UI setting, not a TF command.

SquatClient embeds Lua 5.1 (gopher-lua, pure Go) as a sandboxed scripting language alongside the TF engine. Scripts are plain .lua files so they can later be synced to a daemon (see AUTOMATION.md).
Everything lives in the global table squat. Each plugin gets its own global environment: globals you assign are private to your plugin, and changing string, table or math never affects other plugins.
All scripts run on one thread, one at a time. You never need locks.

Every call into your code (a trigger, a handler, a timer tick, loading the file) has a budget (about 5 million VM instructions and 500 ms wall-clock by default). Exceeding it aborts that call with an error in the log; the client keeps running and your other handlers still work.
Errors in one plugin never stop another plugin.

A line can be live (just arrived) or replayed (scrollback/backlog re-processed after reattaching). Replayed lines only get display effects: gag, highlight colours, and spans returned by line handlers. On replayed lines:
trigger fn callbacks are not called;

line/prompt handlers are called (with l.live == false) so they can restyle or gag, but squat.send, echo, notify, tf, var.set, var.del, after, timer, on, trigger, alias and remove do nothing and return false.
Write line handlers so they compute the display result from the text, and put side effects in trigger fns.

Available: base functions (pairs, pcall, error, setmetatable, tostring, unpack ...), string, table, math, coroutine, and a restricted os with only time, date, clock, difftime (driven by the client clock). print(...) goes to the log.

Not available: io, debug, package, os.execute/remove/rename/getenv/exit, dofile, loadfile, string.dump, getfenv/setfenv, module, newproxy, native modules. loadstring/load work but compile into your own environment and refuse binary chunks. string.rep results are capped (4 MiB).
require("name") loads name.lua (dots become /) from your plugin's own directory only.
squat.send(text [, world]) Send a line to the game. Returns true, or nil, err.
squat.echo(x [, world]) Show text locally. x is a string, one span {s="..."}, or an array of spans/strings.
squat.log(text [, level]) Write to the client log; level is "info", "warn" or "error".
squat.world() Display name of the world the current line/event belongs to.
squat.now() Seconds since the Unix epoch (float) from the client clock.
world defaults to the world of the line/event being handled (timers remember the world they were created in). Calling send/echo/tf with no current world and no world argument is an error.
A span is a table: {s="text", fg=..., bg=..., b=true, dim=, i=, u=, st=, blink=, rev=, link="url"}.
fg/bg is an integer 0-255 (xterm-256 palette index; 0-15 follow the theme) or a string "#rrggbb" for 24-bit truecolor. Both survive the round trip to the display exactly; no quantisation.
prompt the same, only for flushed prompts
connect, disconnect {world, ...} (fields chosen by the engine)
gmcp {package, data, raw, world} (data is the decoded JSON)
input {text, world}; return true to swallow the input
Line handlers may modify the line:
squat.on("line", function(l) if l.text:find("spam") then return {gag = true} end l.spans = {{s = "[!] ", fg = 196}, unpack(l.spans)} -- assign a new table (in-place edits are not seen) end)
Return {gag=true} to hide the line, {spans=...} to replace it, {stop=true} to stop later rules. A gag does not stop later rules (so a gagged line can still trigger an auto-heal).
Ordering: triggers and line handlers form one list, run by priority (higher first, default 0), then in registration order. This is deterministic and identical on live and replayed lines.
squat.on returns an id; squat.remove(id) (alias squat.cancel) unregisters it.

squat.trigger{ match = "You are hit by * for * damage.", -- glob unless regex=true regex = false, -- true: RE2 regular expression (unanchored search) icase = false, -- case-insensitive gag = false, -- hide the line (display effect, also on replay) fg = "#ff8800", bg = 17, b = true, u = true, -- highlight (display effect, also on replay) hilite = "line", -- "line" (default) or "match": colour only the matched text world = "MyMUSH", -- optional: only this world (name or id) priority = 0, fn = function(m) ... end, -- optional, live lines only }

Glob: matches the whole line; matches any run (captured), ? one character, \ and \? are literal. Regex: Go RE2 syntax (<https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax>): linear-time, no backreferences or lookaround; named groups (?P<name>...).
fn(m) gets m.text, m[0] (whole match), m[1..n] (captures; "" if a group did not take part), m.named.<name>, m.world, m.live, m.spans, m.prompt. It may return {gag=true}/{spans=...}/{stop=true}.
Aliases run on text the user typed:
squat.alias{match = "k *", fn = function(m) squat.send("kill " .. m[1]) end}
Same match options (regex, icase, world, priority). An alias handles the input (it is not sent) unless its function returns false; the first handling alias wins.
squat.timer{every = 30, count = 5, fn = function() ... end} -- count omitted: repeat forever squat.after(2.5, function() ... end) -- once local id = squat.timer{...}; squat.cancel(id)

Intervals are seconds (minimum 0.05 by default, at most 512 live timers). Timers are scheduled through the client host and use its clock; they are removed on plugin reload. A tick that errors is logged and the timer keeps going.

squat.var.get(name [, default]), squat.var.set(name, value), squat.var.del(name), squat.var.keys(). Values are strings, numbers, booleans, or tables of those (JSON-compatible; functions and cycles are rejected). set(name, nil) deletes. The store belongs to the engine, is shared by all plugins (prefix your names), survives /reload, and is exported/imported as JSON (Runtime.ExportVars/ImportVars).
squat.regex.match(pattern, text) returns nil or a table m[0], m[1..n], m.named; squat.regex.test(pattern, text) returns a boolean; squat.regex.replace(pattern, text, repl) uses $1/${name}.

squat.tf(code [, world]) runs one line of TinyFugue input in the TF engine (true or nil, err). TF's /lua <code> runs Lua in a persistent console environment (engine wiring: Runtime.Exec, or Runtime.ExecInCallback when TF was itself called from Lua).

plugins/ heal.lua a single-file plugin named "heal" combat/ plugin.json {"name": "combat", "version": "1.0", "description": "...", "enabled": true, "main": "main.lua"} main.lua entry point (default main.lua, then init.lua) util.lua require("util")

plugin.json is optional; "enabled": false skips the plugin. A plugin that fails to load is reported and skipped. /reload discards all handlers, timers and plugin globals and re-runs every plugin from disk.
The scripts below are in testdata/lua/ and are exercised by the test suite.

squat.trigger{ match = "^HP: (\\d+)/(\\d+)", regex = true, fn = function(m) local hp, max = tonumber(m[1]), tonumber(m[2]) if hp / max < 0.4 and squat.now() - squat.var.get("last_heal", 0) > 3 then squat.var.set("last_heal", squat.now()) squat.send("cast heal") end end, }
squat.trigger{match = "*tells you*", fg = "#ff8800", b = true} squat.trigger{match = "treasure", regex = true, hilite = "match", fg = "#ffd700", bg = 52}
Gag spam (still counting it on live lines):
squat.trigger{match = "^<Spam> ", regex = true, gag = true, fn = function() squat.var.set("spam_count", squat.var.get("spam_count", 0) + 1) end}
squat.on("connect", function() squat.timer{every = 300, fn = function() squat.send("") end} end)
squat.alias{match = "k *", fn = function(m) squat.send("kill " .. m[1]) end}
squat.trigger{match = "* arrives.", fn = function(m) squat.tf("/echo -aB Welcome, " .. m[1] .. "!") end}
Limits (what the budget can and cannot stop)

Enforced per call: VM instruction count (main thread), wall-clock timeout (also stops coroutines), heap-growth ceiling (sampled every 65536 instructions, process-wide so approximate), Lua call depth and stack size, string.rep size, timer/variable counts. Not interruptible: a single long-running built-in such as a pathological string.find pattern or very wide string.format; the call is marked failed when it returns, but it can still occupy the (single) script thread until then. Prefer squat.regex (RE2, linear time) for untrusted patterns.
